description: We are a STEM-focused team from Miami Dade College's Padron Campus, bringing together students interested in computer science, mechanical engineering, technology, and innovation. We enjoy coding, designing, building new things, and solving challenging problems. Our goal is to collaborate, learn from each other, and develop a creative, functional solution for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
Earth Data Detective: Florida is a free trip planner powered by NASA climate trends. You choose a place in Florida, an activity (theme parks, beach, off-roading, or hiking and camping) and the year of your trip. The app scores every month from 0 to 100, explains why, and warns about heat-danger months and hurricane season.

Behind every score is the challenge itself: trend detection. For each place and each month of the year (for example, every July since 1981), we test 45 years of NASA data for a statistically significant trend in temperature, rain and humidity (dew point). If a trend is proven, the planner carries it forward to the trip year. If not, it uses the average of the last 15 years instead of guessing. Users can open the evidence for any month: the chart, the trend line and how sure we are.


Why it matters: Florida is getting hotter and muggier, but the evidence sits in research papers and spreadsheets, usually in English only. About one in three Floridians speaks another language at home, and about two million work outdoors. Our tool turns NASA data into plain answers that tourists, families, outdoor workers and students can use.
details:
Earth Data Detective: Florida is a free website that turns 45 years of NASA climate data into plain answers. Its main feature is a trip planner. You pick a place in Florida, an activity (theme parks, beach, off-roading, or hiking and camping) and the year of your trip. The planner scores every month from 0 to 100, explains why, and warns you about heat-danger months and hurricane season.

Behind every score is trend detection, which is what the challenge asks for:

  1. We use monthly NASA MERRA-2 data (air temperature, rainfall and dew point) from NASA POWER, from 1981 to 2025, and monthly sea level from 14 NOAA tide gauges.
  2. We remove the seasons by comparing each month only with the same month in other years.
  3. We test each place, and each calendar month, for a trend:
    • the Mann-Kendall test checks whether a trend is real;
    • Sen’s slope measures the speed of change per decade;
    • a linear regression with a 95% confidence interval and a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation back up the result.
  4. Every result says how sure we are: “Very sure” (p < 0.05), “Not sure yet” (0.05 to 0.25) or “No real evidence” (above 0.25).
  5. For the trip year, the planner continues a trend only if it is proven. Otherwise it uses the average of the last 15 years. It also shows the range that 8 out of 10 past years fell into.

The other tabs:

  • My area: the answers for 13 places (Is it getting hotter, rainier or muggier? Is the sea rising?).
  • Florida map: where the state is changing fastest.
  • Compare places: two places side by side.
  • Beginner’s guide: how to read a trend, with a “Trend or luck?” simulator.
  • The whole site works in English, Spanish and Haitian Creole.

Benefits

  • Plain answers in everyday language, with a clear “how sure are we” for every result.
  • Free, works on any phone, no account needed.
  • Three languages, switched with one click.
  • It teaches people how to judge a trend, not just what the answer is.
  • It is honest about limits: it shows uncertainty, labels our comfort rules as our own and not NASA science, and says a trend shows that something changed, not why.
  • Anyone can download the data behind each chart.

Intended impact
Florida is getting hotter and muggier and the sea is rising, but the evidence usually sits in research papers and spreadsheets, in English only. About one in three Floridians speaks another language at home, and about two million people in Florida work outdoors. Our tool helps:

  • Tourists and families pick safer, better dates.
  • Outdoor workers (farms, construction, landscaping) see which months are heat-danger months.
  • Coastal residents see how fast the sea is rising at their nearest tide gauge, which helps explain high-tide flooding.
  • Spanish and Haitian Creole speakers get the same information in their own language.
  • Teachers and students get a free lesson on reading real NASA data.

Tools, languages and software

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the static website, with Plotly.js for charts and maps and OpenStreetMap for map tiles.
  • Python to download and prepare the data and to check the statistics.
  • GitHub to store the code and Vercel to host the site.
  • Microsoft Excel for the team’s analysis workbook.
  • Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant for coding and translations.
  • No special hardware: everything runs in a web browser.

How it is creative
Instead of another climate chart, we built trend detection into a decision people already make: when to plan a trip or an outdoor activity. Each month gets its own trend test, so the planner can show how a specific month, like July in Orlando, is changing. The “Trend or luck?” simulator lets users act as the scientist: we hide a trend in made-up weather and they watch whether the test can find it. And offering everything in Haitian Creole is rare for climate tools, even though Florida has the largest Haitian community in the United States.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty: we only continue a trend when it is statistically significant; otherwise we use recent averages.
  • Checking the data: we compared NASA results with NOAA weather stations and PSMSL tide gauges. Temperature and sea level agree. Rain disagrees in Miami and Tampa, so we label rain as the least certain variable instead of hiding it.
  • Seasons: we compare each month only with the same month in other years, so normal summer heat is never mistaken for a trend.
  • Accessibility: plain language, three languages, a version that works well on phones, and a beginner’s guide.
  • Heat: we track dew point (how muggy the air is) because heat plus humidity is Florida’s real health danger, and we flag heat-danger months.
  • Limits: the site is not a weather forecast, it doesn’t measure storms, and each data square covers about 50 km (30 miles), so it describes an area, not one street. The site says all of this.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources)
projectRefs: NOAA Tides and Currents (CO-OPS), monthly mean sea level for 14 Florida tide gauges
